Stripetail rockfish (Sebastes saxicola) is a relatively small-bodied scorpaenid that inhabits the continental shelf from southern California to central Baja California, where it is frequently taken as bycatch in bottom trawl surveys. Examination of otoliths from museum specimens indicates that the oldest documented individuals live for approximately 13,870 days at a water temperature of 6.5 °C [T = 6.5 °C], a longevity estimate that corresponds to about thirty-eight years [am = about thirty-eight years] when expressed in annual terms. This lifespan is noteworthy among nearshore rockfishes, as many congeners of comparable size exhibit maximum ages of only fifteen to twenty-five years. The species attains an ultimate total length of 38 centimeters [Li = 38 centimeters], which is modest relative to the more commercially targeted species such as Sebastes alutus and Sebastes entomelas. Growth trajectories derived from length-at-age data suggest that individuals approach this asymptotic size relatively slowly, a pattern consistent with the conservative life-history strategy observed across much of the genus.

Sexual maturation in Stripetail rockfish occurs at a considerably smaller body size than the species maximum. Field collections indicate that the total length at puberty is approximately 11 centimeters [Lp = approximately 11 centimeters], a threshold that is reached during the second or third year of life. The corresponding wet weight at puberty for a fish of this length is estimated at about 16.5 grams [Wwp = about 16.5 grams], a value derived from the species-specific length-weight relationship. This early maturation relative to ultimate size is a common pattern among short-lived or fast-growing Sebastinae, though it stands in contrast to the delayed maturity seen in deeper-dwelling rockfishes such as Sebastes borealis. The reproductive strategy of Sebastes saxicola is viviparous, with females retaining fertilized eggs internally until parturition. Each newly extruded larva emerges at a remarkably small mass, with the wet weight at birth measuring only 0.000268 grams [Wwb = 0.000268 grams] based on the estimated egg diameter of 0.8 millimeters and the density of a typical teleost ovum.

The species exhibits an annual reproductive cycle that is closely tied to seasonal upwelling patterns and water temperature. Under the thermal regime characteristic of its core habitat, approximately 6.5 °C [T = 6.5 °C], ripe females typically carry between 1,500 and 2,500 developing larvae per brood [N_R_i = between 1,500 and 2,500 developing larvae per brood] during the peak spawning period in late winter. Each female generally produces a single brood per year [F_R_i = single brood per year], a relatively low reproductive frequency compared to the multiple clutches observed in warmer-water rockfishes. The maximum reproductive output of this species, expressed as an annual production rate, is therefore around 630 offspring per year, a figure consistent with the energetic constraints imposed by a cool, low-productivity environment. Maternal body size correlates positively with brood size, with larger females contributing disproportionately to annual recruitment. The reproductive mode, in which developing embryos are nourished solely by yolk reserves, limits the number of offspring that can be gestated simultaneously relative to species that exhibit post-fertilization maternal provisioning.

Scale-based analyses and tag-recapture studies suggest that adult Stripetail rockfish maintain a relatively stable body mass over much of their reproductive lifespan. The ultimate wet weight for a fully grown individual, corresponding to a fish that has reached 38 centimeters [Li = 38 centimeters] total length, is approximately 761 grams [Wwi = approximately 761 grams] under the weight-length relationship for this species. This asymptotic body mass places Sebastes saxicola at the smaller end of the size spectrum for rockfishes, comparable to species such as Sebastes elongatus and Sebastes serranoides. The relationship between length and weight, described by the form W = aL^b with a coefficient of 0.01000 and an exponent of 3.09, indicates a slightly positively allometric growth pattern wherein heavier individuals gain mass more rapidly per unit increase in length. This allometric shift may reflect the ontogenetic acquisition of robust skeletal structures and lipid storage tissues necessary for sustaining reproductive output over multiple seasons. Field observations confirm that most adults weigh between 400 and 700 grams, with 761 grams [Wwi = 761 grams] representing the upper bound of recorded masses.

Comparisons with congeneric species highlight the intermediate life-history position of Stripetail rockfish within the diverse Sebastes clade. While the maximum lifespan of roughly thirteen thousand eight hundred and seventy days [am = roughly thirteen thousand eight hundred and seventy days] under the prevailing temperature conditions of 6.5 °C [T = 6.5 °C] is modest relative to the century-spanning longevity of Sebastes aleutianus or Sebastes borealis, it substantially exceeds the short lifespans of semi-pelagic species such as Sebastes jordani. The wet weight at puberty of 16.5 grams [Wwp = 16.5 grams] represents approximately 2.2 percent of the ultimate wet weight (761 grams) [Wwi = 761 grams], a fractional allocation to early reproduction that is intermediate between the fast-maturing, r-selected species and the highly k-selected, deepwater forms. The small larval mass of 0.000268 grams [Wwb = 0.000268 grams] is typical of viviparous scorpaenids that produce large numbers of tiny, planktonic offspring. The combination of an extended lifespan, moderate asymptotic size, and modest reproductive output per event positions Sebastes saxicola as a species with a relatively conservative demographic strategy, one that is adapted to the stable but low-productivity benthic environments of the outer continental shelf.
